artiest/irving-berlin.text:
Irving Berlin was born in 1888 as Israel Beilin, probably in Tyumen in Siberia, in the Russian Empire. In 1893 his Jewish family arrived in New York via Ellis Island. Berlin became one of the great names of Tin Pan Alley, the street of music publishers in Manhattan. He is an example of the writer as star: not the singer, but the maker of the song came first.

As a boy Berlin sold newspapers and worked as a singing waiter. In 1907 his first published song appeared. The breakthrough came in 1911 with Alexander's Ragtime Band. About a million copies of the sheet music were sold that year, and another million the year after. Despite the title it is more a march than a rag, with little syncopation. Berlin could hardly read music and played the piano only in F-sharp major. For other keys he used a transposing piano. In sixty years he is estimated to have written 1,500 songs, for sheet music, Broadway and Hollywood.

He wrote White Christmas for the film Holiday Inn (1942). Bing Crosby's version is estimated to have sold more than fifty million copies, more than any other single. The song won an Oscar. He also wrote God Bless America (1938) and the musical Annie Get Your Gun (1946), with There's No Business Like Show Business. Berlin died in 1989 in New York, aged 101.
artiest/irving-berlin.listen: Listen to Alexander's Ragtime Band in Louis Armstrong's 1937 version. Berlin's melody moves like a march, with little syncopation. Notice how Armstrong and his orchestra nevertheless put swing into it.

artiest/irving-caesar.text:
Irving Caesar was an American lyricist and composer, mainly for the theatre. He was born on 4 July 1895 in New York as Isidor Keiser, the son of a Romanian-Jewish lawyer. His older brother Arthur became a screenwriter in Hollywood. The brothers grew up in Yorkville, the same Manhattan neighbourhood as the Marx Brothers. Around 1901 Irving wrote his first poem.

In his career he worked with many composers, such as Rudolf Friml, George Gershwin, Sigmund Romberg, Victor Herbert, Ted Koehler and Ray Henderson. He wrote the lyrics of standards such as Swanee, Sometimes I'm Happy and Crazy Rhythm. With Vincent Youmans he wrote I Want to Be Happy and Tea for Two for the musical No, No, Nanette in 1925. The latter is one of the most recorded songs ever. He also worked on revues such as the Greenwich Village Follies from 1922 to 1924.

At the end of the 1930s he wrote a series of children's songs about safety, friendship and health with Gerald Marks. He performed hundreds of times in schools. He sat on the board of ASCAP, the organisation that administers rights for songwriters, for almost thirty years, and co-founded the Songwriters Guild of America. In 1972 he was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. His lyrics are simple and singable, and showed how the American popular song took shape in the theatre of the 1920s. He died in 1996, aged one hundred and one.
artiest/irving-caesar.listen: Listen to a version of Tea for Two and notice the lyric: how simple are the words, and how does the melody make them sound almost effortless?

artiest/isaac-hayes.text: Isaac Hayes was a writer and producer at the soul label Stax in Memphis. With David Porter he wrote hits such as Soul Man. In the late 1960s he became a star himself with long, orchestral soul songs. For the detective film Shaft (1971) he made a double album full of funk and soul. The title song begins with a wah-wah guitar and a lightning-fast hi-hat, followed by horns, strings and Hayes's spoken vocals. Theme from Shaft won the Oscar for best song. With it Hayes was the first African American to win an Oscar in a category outside acting. In 1974 he played the lead himself in Truck Turner, for which he also wrote the music.
artiest/isaac-hayes.listen: Notice the wah-wah guitar, the fast hi-hat and the build-up in which more and more horns and strings join in.

artiest/isata-kanneh-mason.text:
Isata Kanneh-Mason is a British pianist. She was born on 27 May 1996 and grew up in Nottingham, the first child of Stuart Mason, who is of Antiguan descent, and Kadiatu Kanneh, who comes from Sierra Leone and in 2020 wrote the book House of Music: Raising the Kanneh-Masons. She attended the Purcell School and then studied at the Royal Academy of Music, with the Sir Elton John Scholarship. In 2013 she played in Los Angeles with Elton John himself. Her teachers were Joanna MacGregor and Carole Presland.

In 2021 and 2022 she was an ECHO Rising Star and she received the Leonard Bernstein Award. She also won an Opus Klassik as best young artist. In the 2022 and 2023 season she was artist-in-residence at the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. In 2023 she made her solo debut at the BBC Proms with Prokofiev's third piano concerto, accompanied by the BBC National Orchestra of Wales. She often collaborates with her brother, the cellist Sheku Kanneh-Mason.

Her first album was Romance: The Piano Music of Clara Schumann from 2019, followed by Summertime in 2021, Childhood Tales in 2023 and an album of works by Mendelssohn in 2024, among others. Her debut album was devoted to a woman composer, and together with her brother Sheku she is part of a musical family that brought the classical world to the attention of a wide audience.
artiest/isata-kanneh-mason.listen: Listen to a piece by Clara Schumann on Romance and notice the melody in the right hand: where does the piano sing, and where does the playing become faster and more restless?

artiest/ishaq-al-mawsili.text:
Ishaq al-Mawsili was a Persian musician of the Abbasid era: composer, singer and music theorist. He was born around 767, although some sources give 772, and died in March 850 in Baghdad. His father was the well-known singer Ibrahim al-Mawsili. Ishaq received a broad education in music and Islamic sciences and learned from, among others, the singer Atika bint Shuhda and the lutenist Zalzal. He also wrote poetry in a traditional style.

For more than forty years he was court musician and companion to six caliphs, from Harun al-Rashid to al-Mutawakkil. Like his father, he led the conservative current that held to the classical tradition of the Hejaz. As a result he stood opposed to innovators such as Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi and Ziryab, a pupil of his father, whose style later became more popular. It is told that on hearing a group of players he recognised a single out-of-tune string. Later he went blind.

Later sources attribute two to four hundred songs to him, but all his music has been lost. His roughly forty books on music have also not survived, among them the Kitab al-aghani al-kabir, the Great Book of Songs, which became the basis for the work of Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani. Ishaq is seen as the one who set up a theoretical system for Arabic music. He is therefore important above all as an early voice in the history of music theory in the Arab world.
artiest/ishaq-al-mawsili.listen: No music by Ishaq has survived. So listen instead to a recording of an Arabic oud and notice how a single melodic line is spun out with small ornaments, without chords beneath it.

artiest/itamar-golan.text:
Itamar Golan is an Israeli pianist. He was born on 3 August 1970 in Vilnius in Lithuania and moved with his parents to Israel at the age of one. He studied piano with Lara Vodovoz and Emmanuel Krazovsky and gave his first recital when he was seven. From 1985 to 1989, thanks to a scholarship from the America-Israel Cultural Foundation, he was able to continue his studies at the New England Conservatory in Boston, with Leonard Shure and Patricia Zander. He later learned chamber music with Chaim Taub.

Golan began as a soloist and chamber musician in the United States and Israel. He played live or on record with many violinists, cellists and singers, among them Kyung Wha Chung, Janine Jansen, Barbara Hendricks, Maxim Vengerov, Shlomo Mintz, Mischa Maisky and María Dueñas. From 1991 to 1994 he taught at the Manhattan School of Music in New York. He is now professor of chamber music at the Paris Conservatoire.

His discography is broad. It includes violin sonatas, works for clarinet and piano, the album The Rose Album from 2002, the album sax+ in 2011 and Between the Clouds in 2020. Golan thus stands for the type of musician who is rarely in the foreground, but without whom many great soloists would not sound the way they do. In chamber music the pianist makes the other player's sound possible and lets him or her shine.
artiest/itamar-golan.listen: Listen to one of his recordings of a violin sonata and notice how the piano follows the violinist and sometimes leads: who has the melody, and who gives the rhythm?

artiest/itzhak-perlman.text:
Itzhak Perlman is an Israeli-American violinist. He was born on 31 August 1945 in Tel Aviv, to Polish Jewish parents. At four he contracted polio. Since then he has walked with braces and crutches and played seated. At three he heard a recital by Jascha Heifetz on the radio, and that led him to the violin. At five he was admitted to the music academy of Tel Aviv, where he had lessons for eight years with Rivka Goldgart. He gave his first recital at ten.

In 1958 he appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show, and again in 1964, on the same broadcast as the Rolling Stones. He made his debut at Carnegie Hall in 1963 with the Wieniawski concerto and in 1964 won the Leventritt Competition. In 1965 he played for the first time with the New York Philharmonic, the Bruch violin concerto. At the end of the 1960s he began playing in Europe: in 1968 with the London Symphony Orchestra under André Previn and in 1972 with the Berliner Philharmoniker. He also conducted orchestras and in 1981 sang a small role on a recording of Tosca.

Perlman has won sixteen Grammys and four Emmys and in 2015 received the Presidential Medal of Freedom. In 2007 he played at a state dinner for Elizabeth II and in 2009 at the inauguration of Barack Obama. His warm, full tone made him one of the best-known violinists of his generation, even for people who rarely listen to classical music. In this way he brought the violin to a large audience.
artiest/itzhak-perlman.listen: Listen to the Bruch violin concerto and notice the tone in the slow passages: how long does he sustain a note, and how does the colour of the sound change?

artiest/ivie-anderson.text:
Ivie Anderson was an American jazz singer, born on 10 July 1905 in Gilroy, California. She took singing lessons at a convent school and later in Washington. Her career began around 1921 with performances in Los Angeles. In 1924 she toured with the musical Shuffle Along, and in 1925 she performed in Cuba, at the Cotton Club in New York and in Los Angeles, with the orchestras of Paul Howard and Sonny Clay, among others. In 1928 she sang with Clay's orchestra in Australia.

In 1930 and early 1931 she had a twenty-week residency at the Grand Terrace in Chicago, with Earl Hines's orchestra. In 1931 she became the first regular singer with Duke Ellington's orchestra. For more than ten years she travelled with him. Her first recording there was It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing). She also sang in Ellington's musical Jump for Joy. Because of chronic asthma she left the orchestra in 1942. After that she started the restaurant Chicken Shack in Los Angeles. She died in December 1949 of an asthma-related illness.

Anderson sang pop songs and ballads and was the band's scat singer, imitating instruments and sounds. She often appeared in large type on Ellington's posters in the 1930s. A newspaper wrote that she could sing a song so that the audience understood every word, while at the same time joking with the drummer. She was regarded as one of Ellington's best and most versatile singers for the later years.
artiest/ivie-anderson.listen: Listen to It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing) with Ellington and notice the scat passage: which instrumental sounds does the voice try to imitate?

artiest/j-balvin.text:
J Balvin is a Colombian singer and songwriter. His real name is José Álvaro Osorio Balvín and he was born on 7 May 1985 in Medellín, in a family of Spanish and Syrian descent. He grew up with rock such as Metallica and Nirvana and has a Nirvana tattoo on his knee. At sixteen he went to Oklahoma on an exchange programme and then to New York to study English and music. He lived with an aunt on Staten Island and walked dogs. Back in Medellín he began making and distributing music without a record label, together with his DJ and business partner David Rivera Mazo.

His breakthrough came in 2014 with 6 AM, with Farruko, which reached number two on the Billboard Hot Latin Songs chart. Ay Vamos and Ginza followed, and in 2016 the album Energia appeared, with Bobo, Safari and Sigo Extrañándote, among others. In 2017 he made the single Mi Gente with Willy William. Ay Vamos won a Latin Grammy for best urban song, and its video is one of the most watched Latin American clips ever.

His music is mainly reggaeton, but he also experimented with electronica, house, Latin trap and R&B. His first songs were imitations of reggaeton from Puerto Rico; after that he chose a calmer, more minimalist sound. He collaborated with Ozuna and Nicky Jam, among others. In 2020 he was on the Time list of the hundred most influential people in the world. Balvin brought reggaeton from Colombia into international pop and made the genre less dependent on Puerto Rico.
artiest/j-balvin.listen: Listen to Mi Gente and notice the rhythm beneath the vocals: which sound carries the song, and how does the beat differ from an ordinary pop song?

artiest/j-balvin-en-willy-william.text:
J Balvin and Willy William made the worldwide hit Mi Gente together in 2017. J Balvin is a top Colombian artist in Latin pop and reggaeton. Willy William is a French DJ, producer and rapper, born in 1981 in Fréjus to a Guadeloupean father and an Eritrean mother. He grew up in Champagné in the department of Sarthe.

William made his mark in 2003 with the dancefloor hit B Boyz Shake da Body, with DJ Flex, and as the producer of Tragedie, at the time still under the name Lord William. He joined the French collective Collectif Métissé and worked on many songs by other artists. In 2016 he had his first big French solo hit with Ego, from the album Une seule vie.

With Mi Gente he became internationally known in 2017. The song combines Latin music with electronic dance music and also received a remix with Beyoncé. It received a Latin Billboard Music Award and the video clip got more than two billion views. In 2018 it won an MTV Video Music Award for best Latin video and spent twelve weeks in a row at number 1 on Spotify worldwide. With that the song showed that Spanish-language music without an English translation can reach a worldwide audience. In 2018 William also made La La La and worked on Goodbye by David Guetta and Jason Derulo.
artiest/j-balvin-en-willy-william.listen: Listen to Mi Gente and notice the sung chorus and the rhythm: can you hear how Latin music and electronic dance come together, and how the drop falls exactly on the beat?

artiest/j-dilla.text:
J Dilla's real name was James Dewitt Yancey and he was born in 1974 in Detroit. He came from a musical family: his mother was an opera singer, his father a jazz bassist. As a teenager he sat alone in the basement to learn to make beats with a cassette deck and his growing record collection. In 1992 the Detroit musician Amp Fiddler let him work with an Akai MPC, a sampler with drum pads. That device became his instrument.

With classmates he formed the rap group Slum Village, which made its debut in 1997 with Fantastic, Vol. 1. Meanwhile he produced, often under the name Jay Dee, for The Pharcyde, De La Soul, A Tribe Called Quest, Busta Rhymes and Janet Jackson. He belonged to the Soulquarians, with Questlove and D'Angelo, among others, and worked on records by Erykah Badu and Common. Later he made the album Champion Sound (2003) as Jaylib with Madlib. Characteristic of his work are long, melodic loops from old soul records, with breakbeats and vocal samples running through them.

J Dilla suffered from a rare blood disease and lupus. He died in February 2006 at the age of 32, three days after his last album Donuts was released. His influence only became fully visible after his death. His loose, lagging way of programming drums, in which the hits do not fall exactly on the beat, is still imitated by producers and drummers today.
artiest/j-dilla.listen: Listen to Time: The Donut of the Heart and notice the drums: do the hits fall exactly on the beat, or just slightly early and late? Hear how the soul sample keeps returning and gives the track a dreamy feel.

artiest/j-j-johnson.text:
J. J. Johnson, in full James Louis Johnson, was an American jazz trombonist, composer and arranger. He was born on 22 January 1924. He began on piano at nine and chose the trombone at fourteen. In 1941 he began professionally with Clarence Love, then played with Snookum Russell, where the trumpeter Fats Navarro urged him to play in the style of the tenor saxophonist Lester Young. Later he also played with Benny Carter and Count Basie.

He was one of the first trombonists to embrace bebop. In that music the trombone stood in the background, because instruments with valves and keys, such as the trumpet and saxophone, seemed better suited to the high speed and technical demands. In 1946 Dizzy Gillespie encouraged him. After Basie, Johnson played in small bebop groups in New York, in 1947 he toured with Illinois Jacquet, and he recorded as a leader with Max Roach, Sonny Stitt and Bud Powell, among others. In 1947 he took part in a Charlie Parker session for Dial.

In 1954 he founded the Jay and Kai Quintet with the trombonist Kai Winding, which lasted until 1956 and was a musical and commercial success. After that he led small groups of his own, with Bobby Jaspar, Clifford Jordan, Nat Adderley and Freddie Hubbard, among others. His recordings for Blue Note, as a leader and with Miles Davis, are among his best-known work. Johnson showed that the trombone can sound fast and precise, and made the instrument a full voice in bebop. He died in 2001.
artiest/j-j-johnson.listen: Listen to a recording by Jay and Kai and notice how two trombones play with each other: who takes the melody, who the counter-voice, and how quickly do they switch?

artiest/jack-bruce.text:
Jack Bruce was a Scottish bassist, singer and composer, born in 1943 in Bishopbriggs. As a teenager he played jazz bass and received a scholarship to study cello and composition in Glasgow. In 1962 he went to London to play with Alexis Korner's Blues Incorporated, where he met the drummer Ginger Baker. After that he played in the Graham Bond Organisation, where he switched from double bass to electric bass guitar. After short spells with John Mayall's Bluesbreakers, with Eric Clapton, and with Manfred Mann, he founded Cream in 1966.

In Cream Bruce sang most of the songs and wrote a large part of the music, often with the poet Pete Brown as lyricist. This is how Sunshine of Your Love, White Room and I Feel Free came about. The trio played blues and rock with jazz influences, and in concert let the songs grow into long improvisations. After the end of Cream in 1968 Bruce made solo albums such as Songs for a Tailor (1969) and the free jazz album Things We Like (1970). In 1972 he started the power trio West, Bruce & Laing. He worked with musicians from jazz, fusion and world music, and in 2005 he played with Cream once more at the Royal Albert Hall.

Bruce played his bass not just as accompaniment, but as a full voice alongside guitar and drums. In this way he became one of the most influential bassists in rock, with followers such as Sting, Geddy Lee and Geezer Butler. He died in 2014.
artiest/jack-bruce.listen: Listen to Sunshine of Your Love (1967) by Cream. Notice the riff that bass and guitar play together, and how Bruce plays bass and takes the lead vocal at the same time.

artiest/jack-dejohnette.text: Jack DeJohnette from Chicago began as a pianist and became a drummer. In the 1960s he played in Chicago with AACM musicians, then in Charles Lloyd's quartet with Keith Jarrett. From 1969 to 1972 he was Miles Davis's drummer, including on Bitches Brew. For ECM he recorded with groups of his own, such as Special Edition. From 1983 he was for thirty years the drummer in Keith Jarrett's Standards Trio, with the bassist Gary Peacock. His playing is free and melodic, with a great deal of colour on the cymbals, and suits both standards and free improvisation. He died in 2025.
artiest/jack-dejohnette.listen: Notice the cymbals: a cloud of sound instead of a rigid beat.

artiest/jack-liebeck.text:
Jack Liebeck is a British-German violinist. He was born on 4 August 1980 in London. In 2010 he won a Classical Brit in the category of young British classical performer. BBC Music Magazine spoke of an enchanting silvery tone. His repertoire runs from Mozart's chamber music to contemporary works, such as Brett Dean's violin concerto The Lost Art of Letter Writing from 2008. He also loves science and, among other things, gave the world premiere of a work connected with it.

As a soloist and chamber musician he performed with all the major British orchestras and, beyond them, with the Royal Stockholm Philharmonic Orchestra and the Oslo Philharmonic. He collaborated with Renaud and Gautier Capuçon, Angela Hewitt and Jean-Yves Thibaudet, among others. His debut album, Works for Violin and Piano with Katya Apekisheva, appeared in 2002 and was nominated for a Classical Brit. His Dvořák won the prize for best young artist in 2010. He played the solo in the film music for Jane Eyre from 2011 and for Anna Karenina from 2012.

From 2014 he has recorded for Hyperion, including Kreisler and a series of violin concertos by Bruch, with the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra under Martyn Brabbins. He plays a Guadagnini from 1785, the Ex-Wilhelmj. In 2022 he became artistic director of the Australian Festival of Chamber Music. In this way he is both performer and organiser, and brings romantic and modern repertoire to a wide audience.
artiest/jack-liebeck.listen: Listen to his Bruch and notice the tone of the violin at the beginning: is it silvery and light, or warm and full, and how does that change in the fast sections?

artiest/jack-mcduff.text:
Jack McDuff, born Eugene McDuffy, was an American jazz organist and bandleader. He was born on 17 September 1926 in Champaign, Illinois, and was known as Brother Jack and later as Captain Jack. He began as a bassist, including in Joe Farrell's group, and was encouraged by Willis Jackson, in whose band he also played bass in the late 1950s. Then he switched to the organ and attracted the attention of the label Prestige. Soon he was leading groups of his own, often as an organ trio. He gave the guitarist George Benson his first big chance.

He was at his most prominent in the era of hard bop and soul jazz in the 1960s. At Prestige he recorded many albums, such as his debut Brother Jack in 1960, The Honeydripper in 1961 with Jimmy Forrest and Grant Green, Brother Jack Meets the Boss in 1962 with Gene Ammons and Screamin' in 1962 with Leo Wright and Kenny Burrell. Atlantic followed, and in the 1970s Blue Note. He recorded To Seek a New Home from 1970 in England with the blues shouter Jimmy Witherspoon.

Many jazz musicians had a hard time when interest in jazz and blues declined in the late 1970s and in the 1980s. In 1988 a new period began with The Reentry for Muse, followed by Concord Jazz. George Benson played on Color Me Blue in 1992. McDuff kept working despite health problems and toured Japan in 2000. He died in 2001. He showed how the Hammond organ with a trio can form a swinging, bluesy band.
artiest/jack-mcduff.listen: Listen to The Honeydripper and notice the organ and the guitar: how do they give each other room for a solo, and what role does the saxophone play in it?

artiest/jack-poels.text:
Jack Poels is a Dutch singer, guitarist and harmonica player. He was born on 27 June 1957 in America, a village in Limburg. He is best known as the lead singer of the Limburg dialect band Rowwen Hèze, for which he writes almost all the music and lyrics. From the mid-1970s he sang with the not very successful band Bad Edge. In 1985 he took the place of the singer of The Legendary Texas Four, a band from his own village.

His music is a mixture of folk, Tex-Mex and accordion music. In his lyrics he talks a lot about his own life. On the album Vandaag from 2001 he sings about his newborn little son, on Dageraad from 2003 about his divorce, and Rodus & Lucius is about his life afterwards. The first Rowwen Hèze album is called Blieve Loëpe, and the emblem on the sleeve is by his own hand: the Statue of Liberty with a cigarette, a clog and a jug of beer. He also designed the sleeve of Dageraad.

Since 2003 he has worked with Leon Giesen on the project Holland America Lijn. In 2007 he was appointed a knight in the Order of Orange-Nassau, and the transport company Veolia named a train after him. Since 2009 he has published a poem every two weeks in Dagblad de Limburger. Poels shows that a regional language and a local story can reach a large audience, without the music losing its origins.
artiest/jack-poels.listen: Listen to a song by Rowwen Hèze and notice the accordion and the language: which words do you not understand, and how does the melody still help you grasp the mood?

artiest/jack-white.text:
Jack White is an American musician, guitarist and singer of the rock duo The White Stripes. He was born on 9 July 1975 in Detroit as John Anthony Gillis, the youngest of ten children. He grew up in Mexicantown in the southwest of the city. Three of his older brothers were in a band, and he learned the instruments they left behind, starting with drums at the age of six. In the daytime he worked as an upholsterer and later started a business of his own, Third Man Upholstery. He played drums with the Detroit band Goober & the Peas and in other underground bands.

In the 1990s he met Meg White. They married in 1996, and he took her surname. In 1997 they founded the White Stripes. In 2001 he started the record label and studio Third Man Records, and that same year White Blood Cells became their breakthrough album. After the band split in 2011, he released Blunderbuss solo in 2012 and Lazaretto in 2014. That last album broke the record for the largest number of vinyl LPs sold in the first week since 1991. Later came No Name in 2024 and other albums.

White is known for his technique, his individuality and his use of analogue technology. He won twelve Grammys and in 2010 and 2023 was on Rolling Stone's list of the best guitarists of all time. In 2025 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of the White Stripes. He played a major role in the garage rock and indie rock of the 2000s.
artiest/jack-white.listen: Listen to a song by The White Stripes and notice the line-up: just guitar, drums and vocals. What sound fills the space, and how does his guitar sound compared with a full band?

artiest/jackie-brenston.text:
Jackie Brenston was an American singer and saxophonist from Clarksdale, Mississippi. His exact date of birth is uncertain, somewhere between about 1928 and 1930. After his military service in the army he learned to play tenor saxophone. In 1950 he joined the Kings of Rhythm, Ike Turner's band, as a saxophonist and sometimes as a singer. On B.B. King's advice the band ended up with Sam Phillips in Memphis.

In early March 1951 the band recorded Rocket 88 there, a song about a car. Brenston sang and received the writing credit, while Turner led the band and played piano. Brenston later admitted that the song leaned on Cadillac Boogie by Jimmy Liggins, another jump blues song about a car. The label Chess released the record under the name Jackie Brenston and his Delta Cats, and not under Turner's. The record became a number 1 on the R&B chart. The musicians received 20 dollars each, and Brenston sold his rights to Phillips. With the proceeds Phillips started Sun Records a year later.

The success caused rows in the band, and Brenston went solo. A second hit did not come. He still played in Lowell Fulson's band and later again with Turner, but took to drink and ultimately became a truck driver. He died in 1979. Yet his name remains tied to a record that is often called the first rock 'n' roll record, and which influenced Bill Haley and the Comets.
artiest/jackie-brenston.listen: Listen to Rocket 88 (1951). Notice Brenston's voice, singing enthusiastically about his new car, and the saxophones and distorted guitar that give the record its raw energy.

artiest/jackie-brenston-en-his-delta-cat.text:
Jackie Brenston was an American singer and saxophonist from Clarksdale in Mississippi. His year of birth is uncertain: dates between 1927 and 1930 have been given. After his military service he learned to play tenor saxophone and in 1950 joined Ike Turner and his band the Kings of Rhythm, as a saxophonist and sometimes singer.

In March 1951 the band recorded in Memphis in Sam Phillips's studio, on B.B. King's advice. One of the songs was Rocket 88, on which Brenston sang lead and was credited as the writer. The song leans on the jump blues about a car, and Brenston himself said that it was borrowed from Cadillac Boogie by Jimmy Liggins. Turner insisted that he wrote the music. Phillips licensed the recording to Chess Records in Chicago, which released the record under the name Jackie Brenston and his Delta Cats instead of Turner's. The record reached number 1 on the Billboard R&B chart and sold about half a million copies.

Rocket 88 is regarded as one of the first rock 'n' roll records. Phillips himself said it was the first, although others name other records. The success paid for Sun Records, which Phillips started a year later. The music blends the rhythms of jump blues with a heavy, distorted guitar and a swinging saxophone. Brenston left the band afterwards and had little further success. He died in 1979.
artiest/jackie-brenston-en-his-delta-cat.listen: Listen to Rocket 88 and notice the guitar sound and the saxophone: the guitar sounds dirty and distorted, the sax swings over it. Do you hear a forerunner of rock 'n' roll?

artiest/jackie-mclean.text:
Jackie McLean was an American alto saxophonist, composer, bandleader and teacher. He was born on 17 May 1931 in Harlem. His father played guitar in Tiny Bradshaw's orchestra and died in 1939. After that Jackie was taught by his godfather, his stepfather, who owned a record shop, and a number of well-known teachers. Neighbours such as Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell gave him informal lessons. In 1951, at twenty years old, he played together with Sonny Rollins on Miles Davis's album Dig. He also recorded with Gene Ammons, with Charles Mingus for Pithecanthropus Erectus and with Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers.

His first records as a leader fall under hard bop. Later he became an interpreter of modal jazz, without letting go of his hard bop base. He was known for a tone of his own, which resembled that of a tenor saxophone and was often called bittersweet, piercing or searing, with a slightly sharp tuning and a strong feeling for the blues. In 1962 he recorded Let Freedom Ring for Blue Note, in which he combined ideas from Ornette Coleman's free jazz with hard bop. He had a good eye for talent and supported Tina Brooks, Charles Tolliver and Larry Willis, among others.

In 1967 Blue Note ended his contract and he concentrated on touring. From 1968 he taught at the Hartt School of the University of Hartford and in 1970 he founded, with his wife Dollie and the bassist Paul Brown, the Artists Collective in Hartford, an organisation for the culture of the African diaspora. In 2001 he received the American Jazz Masters fellowship. He died in 2006 and was inducted into the DownBeat Hall of Fame that year.
artiest/jackie-mclean.listen: Listen to Let Freedom Ring and notice the tone of his alto saxophone: what sounds sharp and searing, and where does he break out of the harmonic framework?

artiest/jackie-wilson.text:
Jackie Wilson was an American singer, born in 1934 in Highland Park, an enclave of Detroit. As a boy he sang in church with his mother and later in a gospel group. As a teenager he also boxed, but singing won. In 1953 he became lead singer of Billy Ward and His Dominoes, succeeding Clyde McPhatter, from whom he learned a great deal. In 1957 he began a solo career at the label Brunswick.

His first solo single was Reet Petite (1957), written by Berry Gordy, Gwendolyn Gordy and Billy Davis. That trio then made more records for him, with Lonely Teardrops (1958) as the high point, which topped the R&B chart. With the money Gordy earned from those songs, he started his studio Hitsville USA in Detroit, the base of Motown. Wilson himself afterwards also sang operatic ballads such as Night. In 1963 he had success with Baby Workout, and in 1967 with (Your Love Keeps Lifting Me) Higher and Higher, recorded with the Motown musicians.

Wilson had a voice with a range of several octaves and was known as Mr. Excitement. On stage he did splits, spins and jumps. With that he inspired James Brown, Michael Jackson and Elvis Presley, who became friends with him. In this way he played a part in the transition from rhythm and blues to soul. In 1975 he suffered a heart attack during a performance. He never regained consciousness and died in 1984.
artiest/jackie-wilson.listen: Listen to Lonely Teardrops (1958). Notice how Wilson shoots his voice from low to high and how the backing vocals keep spurring him on.

artiest/jaco-pastorius.text: Jaco Pastorius grew up in Florida and played a fretless bass guitar. This allowed him to play gliding notes and made his bass sound singing. He also played harmonics, high overtones. His first album Jaco Pastorius (1976) opens with Charlie Parker's Donna Lee, on bass and percussion alone. From 1976 to 1981 he played in Weather Report and wrote Teen Town, among other pieces. He also worked with Joni Mitchell and Pat Metheny. Pastorius changed the role of the bass guitar in jazz. He suffered from bipolar disorder and died in 1987 after a violent altercation with a bouncer.
artiest/jaco-pastorius.listen: Hear how the bass guitar plays the melody and sings like a horn.

artiest/jacob-collier.text:
Jacob Collier is an English singer, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist, producer and teacher. He was born on 2 August 1994 and grew up in north London. His mother Suzie Collier is a violinist, conductor and teacher at the Junior Academy of the Royal Academy of Music, and his grandfather was a violinist. At home they sang Bach chorales. At ten he played Tiny Tim in the 2004 film A Christmas Carol. He attended the Purcell School and briefly studied jazz piano at the Royal Academy.

In 2011 he began uploading home-made videos to YouTube, first with a vocal arrangement of Pure Imagination, in 2013 with a version of Stevie Wonder's Don't You Worry 'bout a Thing. He played and sang all the parts himself, in split-screen footage. In 2014 he became friends with Herbie Hancock and Quincy Jones. He remained independent and made his first album himself. In 2017 he won Grammys for his arrangements of the Flintstones theme and Wonder's You and I.

From 2018 he worked on Djesse, an album in four parts and fifty songs with more than twenty artists and ensembles. The first part, with the Metropole Orkest, appeared in December 2018. His music combines jazz with other genres and makes much use of reharmonisation and dense harmonies. In his live shows, with circles of instruments and loop stations, he gets the audience to sing. Collier showed that a young musician could reach an audience of his own via the internet and that harmony can captivate an audience.
artiest/jacob-collier.listen: Listen to his version of You and I and notice the chords beneath the melody: where does a harmony surprise you, and how many voices do you hear at once?

artiest/jacob-do-bandolim.text:
Jacob do Bandolim, born Jacob Pick Bittencourt, was a Brazilian composer and mandolin player. He was born in 1918 in Rio de Janeiro, the son of a Brazilian-Jewish mother and a non-Jewish father. His stage name means Jacob of the mandolin, after his instrument. He died in 1969 of a heart attack, on the way back from a day with his friend Pixinguinha, with whom he wanted to plan a recording.

Jacob was known as a perfectionist. With his group Época de Ouro he reached a very high level of performance. He hated the image of the sloppy, drunken folk musician and demanded commitment and a neat appearance from his players, who, like himself, had ordinary jobs. He himself worked as a pharmacist, insurance salesman, street vendor and finally notary, to earn his living alongside his music.

His name is above all tied to choro, the Brazilian instrumental style with fast, playful melodies. He wrote more than a hundred pieces, from the lyrical Noites Cariocas to Receita de Samba and Dôce de Coco, and the sharp, jazzy Assanhado, which is reminiscent of bebop. He also researched the older choro and other Brazilian styles and tried to preserve them. His son Sérgio Bittencourt later wrote the song Naquela Mesa as a tribute to his father.
artiest/jacob-do-bandolim.listen: Listen to Noites Cariocas and follow the mandolin: notice the singing melody and the guitars that sit beneath it rhythmically.

artiest/jacob-miller.text:
Jacob Miller was a Jamaican reggae singer, born on 4 May 1952 in Mandeville. He was the only son of Joan Ashman, a choir singer and pianist. He grew up as a Rastafarian and was raised mainly by his great-aunt. At a young age he moved to Kingston and hung around the recording studios, especially Clement Coxsone Dodd's Studio One. He hoped to become the next child star there. At thirteen he recorded three songs for Dodd, including Love is a Message. It was not a success.

In 1974 Augustus Pablo, who ran the sound system label Rockers with his brother Garth, recorded a version of that song: Keep on Knocking. Over the next year and a half Miller sang for Pablo Baby I Love You So, False Rasta, Who Say Jah No Dread and Each One Teach One, among others. He became the singer of Inner Circle, a roots reggae band that became known for covers of American hits, with Roger Lewis on guitar and Ian Lewis on bass. Alongside Inner Circle he kept recording solo, including I'm a Natty, a version of the Wailers' Soul Rebel.

His best-known recording is the dub track King Tubby Meets The Rockers Uptown with Augustus Pablo, a dub of Baby I Love You So, made by King Tubby. AllMusic called the vocal version a masterpiece. Miller died on 23 March 1980 in a car accident. He showed how a singer with a cheerful, playful voice could deliver deep roots reggae and how dub could completely renew a song.
artiest/jacob-miller.listen: Listen to Baby I Love You So and then to King Tubby Meets The Rockers Uptown. What is left of the vocals in the dub, and what do bass and drums do with the space?

artiest/jacopo-peri.text:
Jacopo Peri was an Italian composer, singer and instrumentalist of the late Renaissance and early Baroque. He was born in 1561 in Rome or Florence and died in 1633. He sang in churches in Florence, including in the monastery of Santissima Annunziata, and from 1588 worked at the Medici court, first as a tenor and keyboard player and later as a composer. His nickname was Il Zazzerino, the blond.

In the 1590s he joined Jacopo Corsi, an important patron of music. They wanted to bring Greek tragedy back to life, and built on the experiments of the Florentine Camerata with monody: solo singing above a basso continuo. With the poet Ottavio Rinuccini, Peri made Dafne around 1597, the first work in a new form, opera. It has largely been lost.

His second opera, Euridice, was first performed on 6 October 1600 in the Palazzo Pitti, at the wedding of Maria de' Medici and Henry IV of France. This is the oldest opera that has survived. The work uses recitatives that move the action along between the arias and choruses. The singer tells the story in a speech-like singing style, just above a simple accompaniment. Peri wrote more operas, including La Flora with Marco da Gagliano, but his style was already considered old-fashioned at his death. Even so he is important as the man who began music theatre with song and story.
artiest/jacopo-peri.listen: Listen to Funeste piagge from Euridice and notice how the singer almost speaks on the melody. Can you hear how little accompaniment there is beneath the voice, and how the text comes first?

artiest/jacques-arcadelt.text:
Jacques Arcadelt, also Jacob Arcadelt, was a Franco-Flemish Renaissance composer. He was born on 10 August 1507 in Namur, in the Habsburg Netherlands, and died on 14 October 1568 in Paris. As a young man he moved to Italy and by the end of the 1520s he was in Florence, where he could have met Philippe Verdelot, the author of the first attributed madrigals. Around 1538 he moved to Rome, where until 1551 he was a singer and composer in the Sistine Chapel. In 1542 he got to know Michelangelo, but his settings of two of the artist's sonnets were received with indifference.

In 1551 he returned to France. In 1557 he published a book of masses, dedicated to his new employer, Cardinal Charles de Guise, for whom he was choirmaster. He left behind work spanning forty years or more: twenty-four motets, one hundred and twenty-five French chansons, about two hundred and fifty madrigals, three masses and settings of the Lamentations of Jeremiah and the Magnificat. All of it is vocal. Rabelais mentioned him in Gargantua and Pantagruel, between Janequin and Sermisy, in a choir singing a bawdy song.

Arcadelt is regarded as the most influential member of the early, classical phase of the madrigal. Through his publications the madrigal also became known outside Italy. His first book of madrigals was often reprinted and later used as a model, because later composers saw his style as an ideal. His music shows how a poem and a melody can become one whole in a few voices.
artiest/jacques-arcadelt.listen: Listen to a madrigal by Arcadelt and notice how the voices alternate: which voice takes over the text, and when do they all sing together?

artiest/jacques-brel.text:
Jacques Brel was born in 1929 in Schaerbeek near Brussels, in a French-speaking family of Flemish descent. At school he was no high achiever, but he wrote stories and acted. After school he worked in his father's cardboard factory, a job that bored him. In 1952 he began writing songs and performing in Brussels cabarets. In 1953 he recorded his first record and left for Paris, despite his family's opposition.

In the Paris cabarets he worked hard on his career. The breakthrough came in 1956 with Quand on n'a que l'amour. The pianists François Rauber and Gérard Jouannest became his regular musical partners: Rauber wrote the orchestral arrangements, Jouannest accompanied him on tour. In 1959 La Valse à mille temps appeared, which also included Ne me quitte pas. Around that time he put the guitar aside to concentrate entirely on his singing and acting. His performances were theatrical and emotional, and classics such as Le plat pays, Marieke, Madeleine and Amsterdam brought halls to their feet in standing ovations. He sang mainly in French, sometimes in Dutch.

Brel is regarded as a master of modern chanson. He also became a model for English-language artists such as Scott Walker and David Bowie, and his songs were translated and sung by Nina Simone and Frank Sinatra, among others. He also acted in ten films. He died in 1978.
artiest/jacques-brel.listen: Listen to Ne me quitte pas and notice how Brel uses his voice: whispering and pleading, and then loud and desperate. Hear how the accompaniment moves along with him.

artiest/jacques-morali.text:
Jacques Morali was a French producer and songwriter of disco and dance music. He was born in 1947 in Casablanca, in a Jewish Moroccan family. In the late 1960s he wrote music in Paris for orchestras and for the Crazy Horse, and also released a single of his own. In the early 1970s he met the producer Henri Belolo. Because his success in France was disappointing, he tried his luck in America.

In 1975 Morali wanted to turn Brazil, a song from a film with Carmen Miranda, into a grand club track with powerful female singers. Belolo paid for his stay at Sigma Sound Studios in Philadelphia, and so the Ritchie Family came into being. After that came The Best Disco in Town (1976), among others. In New York Morali visited a costume party at a gay disco in Greenwich Village. There he got the idea for a group of singers and dancers who each played a different gay fantasy figure. This is how Village People came about, with San Francisco (You've Got Me) (1977), Macho Man and YMCA (1978), In the Navy (1979) and Go West (1980).

Morali's music had simple arrangements, simple lyrics and melodies you remember at once, with a healthy dose of camp. Between 1974 and 1982 he recorded more than 65 albums and wrote for artists such as Cher, Dalida and Patrick Juvet. He showed how a producer could devise a group from beginning to end. Morali contracted HIV in the mid-1980s and died in 1991 in Paris of the consequences of AIDS.
artiest/jacques-morali.listen: Listen to Macho Man by Village People. Notice the simple melody and the repeated chorus, and how the disco beat pushes the whole song steadily forward.

artiest/jacques-offenbach.text:
Jacques Offenbach was a French composer, cellist and impresario, born in Germany. He was born in 1819 in Cologne, the son of a synagogue cantor. At fourteen he entered the conservatoire in Paris, but he left it after a year and stayed in the city. From 1835 to 1855 he earned his living as a cellist and conductor, and became internationally known. His real ambition was comic music for the theatre.

Because the Opéra-Comique would not perform him, in 1855 he rented a small theatre on the Champs-Élysées. There in three years he brought out more than twenty small pieces, many of which became popular. In 1858 followed his first full-length operetta, Orphée aux enfers, with the famous can-can. The work was a great success and is still the most often performed. In the 1860s followed La belle Hélène (1864), La Vie parisienne (1866), La Grande-Duchesse de Gérolstein (1867) and La Périchole (1868). They were also performed in Vienna, London and the United States.

The pieces combine spicy humour about love intrigues with mild satire, often of the empire of Napoleon III, and infectious melodies. In all he wrote almost a hundred operettas. He influenced Franz von Suppé, Johann Strauss II and Arthur Sullivan. His last work, the opera The Tales of Hoffmann, remained unfinished when he died in 1880. It is now frequently performed in adapted versions.
artiest/jacques-offenbach.listen: Listen to the Galop infernal from Orphée aux enfers and notice the tempo: how the music gets faster and wilder, and how the recognisable can-can melody drives the orchestra on.

artiest/jakob-lindberg.text:
Jakob Lindberg is a Swedish lutenist. He was born on 16 October 1952 in Djursholm. His first inspiration was the music of The Beatles and he began with guitar. At fourteen he was taught by Jörgen Rörby, who also introduced him to the lute. He studied music at the University of Stockholm and then at the Royal College of Music in London, with Diana Poulton for lute and Carlos Bonell for classical guitar. There he chose Renaissance and Baroque music on historical instruments.

In 1979 he became lute teacher at the Royal College of Music, succeeding Poulton. He plays solo and in small and large ensembles and also directs operas, with instruments from the lute and guitar families. He recorded music that had never been recorded before, mainly for the label BIS. Among it are Italian chitarrone collections, music by Scottish composers, work by Bach and the first ever recording of the complete solo lute music of John Dowland. In 1985 he founded the Dowland Consort, which plays music from the time of Elizabeth and James, in particular by Dowland and Sylvius Leopold Weiss. As a continuo player on theorbo, chitarrone and archlute he played with ensembles such as The English Concert and the Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment.

For his recordings he uses a lute by Sixtus Rauwolf of Augsburg from around 1590, possibly the oldest lute in the world that can still be played. In 1983 he played the lute himself in the Doctor Who episode The King's Demons. Lindberg showed how much music from around 1600 is still to be discovered.
artiest/jakob-lindberg.listen: Listen to his Dowland on lute and notice the silence between the notes: how long does a string ring, and how does the player fill the space with ornaments?

artiest/jamai-loman.text:
Jamai Loman is a Dutch singer, musical actor and presenter. He was born on 30 June 1986 and grew up in Schoonhoven, with his parents and two older sisters. His artistic path began with a school musical. In 2000 he performed at his school's Shownight and he was in the school jazz band 8CC. In 2003 he took part in Idols, the Dutch version of Pop Idol, and to his own surprise won the first series. At the World Idol of 2003 he received only thirty-six points and finished last, with a critical assessment from the jury.

After his third single he chose the stage over the record industry. He appeared in musicals such as Doornroosje, Hello, Dolly! and Jesus Christ Superstar. In January 2007 he took on the role of the Wiz and alternated as the Scarecrow in the musical The Wiz. In 2008 he played Marius in the Dutch revival of Les Misérables, and he received a John Kraaijkamp Musical Award for best supporting role in a major musical for it. In 2009 he appeared in Urinetown by M-Lab.

Later he became a television personality. From 2016 he was on the jury of Idols. In 2021 he won the third series of The Masked Singer as Cupid, in 2022 he co-presented Lego Masters, and in February 2026 he won the final of the programme Maestro. Loman showed that a talent contest could be a stepping stone to a broad career on stage and television, even though his pop career was short.
artiest/jamai-loman.listen: Listen to his recordings from Idols and then to a musical excerpt with his voice. Notice the difference: where does the voice sound like a pop singer, and where like an actor telling a story?

artiest/james-bernard.text: James Bernard studied at the Royal College of Music in London and worked as an assistant to Benjamin Britten. Starting with The Quatermass Xperiment (1955), written for strings and percussion only, he became the house composer of Hammer Films. He wrote the music for The Curse of Frankenstein (1957), Dracula (1958) and much later Hammer horror. His Dracula theme is built on three heavy notes, which follow the rhythm of the name Dra-cu-la. Bernard worked with hard brass stabs, dissonant chords and racing strings. That loud, direct style became the sound of British horror film of the 1950s and 1960s.
artiest/james-bernard.listen: Find the three-note Dracula motif in the brass and notice the shrill dissonances and racing strings.

artiest/james-brown.text:
James Brown was born in 1933 in Barnwell, South Carolina, and grew up in Augusta, Georgia. He is called the Godfather of Soul, but his greatest contribution lies in rhythm. Brown pushed melody and harmony into the background and made every instrument a kind of percussion. In this way he laid the foundation for funk, and later for a large part of hip hop.

In 1954 he joined Bobby Byrd's group, which became The Famous Flames. Please, Please, Please (1956) became their first rhythm and blues success, and the live album Live at the Apollo (1963) showed what Brown did on stage. In 1965 came Papa's Got a Brand New Bag, his first top ten hit on the pop chart, and I Got You (I Feel Good), with a scream as its hook and horns playing short stabs. Cold Sweat (1967) is often called the first true funk song. After the murder of Martin Luther King he recorded Say It Loud – I'm Black and I'm Proud (1968), which became a civil rights movement anthem. Around 1970 a new band accompanied him, The J.B.'s, with the young bassist Bootsy Collins.

Brown is often called the most sampled artist in the world. Clyde Stubblefield's drum break in Funky Drummer (1970) became the basis of hundreds of hip hop tracks, and Public Enemy built Fight the Power on his grooves. In 1986 Brown was among the first ten names inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. He died on Christmas Day 2006 in Atlanta.
artiest/james-brown.listen: Get Up (I Feel Like Being a) Sex Machine revolves around a single riff by the bassist Bootsy Collins, the guitarist Catfish Collins and the drummer Jabo Starks. Listen to how the guitar keeps repeating the same short stroke, and how Brown calls and Bobby Byrd answers: call and response from church, on the dance floor.

artiest/james-carter-and-the-prisoners.text:
James Carter was an American singer, born in 1925 as the son of a sharecropper in Mississippi. As a young man he was in that state's prison several times. In 1959 he was in Camp B of Parchman Farm, the state penitentiary near Lambert. There Alan Lomax and Shirley Collins recorded him in stereo as he led a group of prisoners in Po' Lazarus. It is a bad man ballad and at the same time a work song: the men chopped wood in the rhythm of the music.

The recording appeared with a well-known sleeve photo of prisoners in striped uniforms on volume nine, Bad Man Ballads, of Lomax's Southern Journey series on Prestige Records. Forty years later the song found a new audience when it was used in the film O Brother, Where Art Thou? by the Coen brothers, with music produced by T-Bone Burnett. The soundtrack topped the Billboard chart for weeks and won a Grammy for Album of the Year.

The Lomax family and Burnett looked for Carter and found him in Chicago, where he had worked as a shipping clerk. He no longer remembered having sung the song. He received a royalty cheque and attended the Grammy ceremony. The other prisoners have never been identified, which is why the soundtrack says James Carter & the Prisoners. Carter died in 2003. The recording matters as testimony to Black work songs, out of which the blues and later much popular music grew.
artiest/james-carter-and-the-prisoners.listen: Listen to Po' Lazarus and notice the axe strokes and the call and response between the lead singer and the group: can you hear how the work sets the beat?

artiest/james-ferraro.text:
James Ferraro is an American musician, producer, composer and visual artist, born in 1986 in Rochester, New York. His father was a musician and DJ, his mother a singer. At eighteen he moved to San Diego, where he met Spencer Clark. Together they formed the noise duo the Skaters around 2006, which released its last record in 2008 with Physicalities Of The Sensibilities Of Ingrediential Stairways. The critic Simon Reynolds said the group had set an international post-noise network in motion.

After that Ferraro released solo records under many names, often on labels of his own such as New Age Tapes and Muscleworks Inc. In 2010 Night Dolls with Hairspray appeared. In 2011 he joined the label Hippos in Tanks, where the controversial album Far Side Virtual was chosen Album of the Year by The Wire. That album marked the transition from a lo-fi sound to a clearer, more electronic one. Collaborations followed later, including with Yves Tumor on Bodyguard and with Bladee on Cold Visions.

Ferraro is regarded as a pioneer of post-noise, hypnagogic pop and vaporwave, genres of the twenty-first century. His work is about hyperreality and consumer culture and draws on contemporary classical music, new age, electronica, drone, sound collages, R&B and hip hop. It sounds like the music of shopping malls, phones and commercials, but estranged. In this way he had a great influence on the internet music of the past decade.
artiest/james-ferraro.listen: Listen to Global Lunch and notice the glossy, artificial sounds: does it sound like music from a commercial or a computer game, and what makes it strange?

artiest/james-horner.text: James Horner (1953–2015) studied at the Royal College of Music in London and then in Los Angeles. He began on cheap films by the producer Roger Corman. Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan (1982) made him known, with romantic orchestral music full of brass fanfares. In Aliens (1986) he built tension with hard, mechanical percussion. Horner loved Celtic sounds: in Braveheart (1995) and Titanic (1997) you hear bagpipes, whistles and a wordless singing voice. Titanic won him two Oscars, for the score and for the song My Heart Will Go On. He sometimes borrowed melodies from classical works. Horner was killed in a plane crash in 2015.
artiest/james-horner.listen: Notice the Celtic instruments, such as uilleann pipes and tin whistle, above a warm string orchestra and a floating choir.
